opus-5.5.text:
I think the clearest place is sample efficiency. A human can see something a handful of times, sometimes once, and really get it, in a way that transfers to new situations. Gradient descent on current architectures typically needs vastly more data to reach comparable competence. If you look at how many words a kid hears before they're fluent, it's tens of millions, maybe a hundred million. Language models train on trillions of tokens. That's a gap of several orders of magnitude, and I don't think it's mostly explained by the model just learning more stuff.

What's less clear is *why* that gap exists, and I'm fairly uncertain. Part of it is probably priors. Evolution did an enormous amount of search over learning algorithms and architectures, so a human brain isn't starting from scratch the way a randomly initialized network is. You could view evolution as the outer loop of gradient descent and lifetime learning as a really well-tuned inner loop. From that angle, the comparison isn't "human learning versus gradient descent." It's "the product of a huge evolutionary optimization versus a fairly generic optimizer we wrote down."

There's also a difference in how learning is structured. Humans learn actively. You choose what to look at, you ask questions, you notice when you're confused and focus there. You rehearse things, you reason about them, and you consolidate them later. Something like gradient descent on a fixed dataset is pretty passive by comparison. Every example gets roughly the same treatment whether it's informative or not. A lot of what looks like humans being smarter learners might be humans being better at curating their own curriculum.

That said, I'd be careful about calling human learning straightforwardly superior. Gradient descent has huge advantages too. It scales. You can parallelize it across enormous amounts of compute. You can copy the result. And once a model is trained, in-context learning already looks surprisingly sample efficient. So you might end up with a system where the slow, data-hungry outer process produces something that learns quickly at runtime, which is structurally a lot like what evolution did with us.

So my rough view is: right now, humans are much better per sample, probably by several orders of magnitude. But I'm not confident that reflects some deep advantage of the brain's algorithm. A lot of it may be the advantage of a very good prior plus active learning, and those are things you can approximate in ML systems over time.

r001.rationale: The response says humans can learn from only a handful of examples and that gradient descent needs vastly more data for comparable competence, estimating a several-orders-of-magnitude gap.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most striking thing is sample efficiency. Humans see vastly less data than a modern language model does, and yet they end up with a model of the world that's in many respects better. A child learns language from, I don't know, tens of millions of words, and GPT-style models are trained on trillions of tokens, and the human comes out with a deeper understanding of a lot of the underlying structure. So on a per-datapoint basis humans are doing something much more efficient.

Now, I want to be a little careful about what's going on there, because there are a couple of candidate explanations and they have different implications. One is that evolution has done a huge amount of work in advance. Humans aren't learning from scratch; they're starting from a prior that was shaped over hundreds of millions of years of selection, and that prior encodes a lot about what kind of world you're in, what kinds of regularities are worth attending to, maybe even quite a bit about language and social reasoning. On that view, gradient descent isn't really worse than human learning; it's that pretraining is playing the role of both evolution and the individual lifetime, and it's just a very expensive way to do the evolution part.

The other explanation is that the within-lifetime learning algorithm is actually better. Humans seem to do a lot of things that gradient descent doesn't obviously do. They actively choose what to pay attention to. They form explicit hypotheses and test them. They can learn something from a single example and then deliberately rehearse it or connect it to things they already know. A lot of that looks less like adjusting weights by a small amount in response to each observation and more like reasoning about what you've seen. And I think the honest answer is that we don't know how much of the gap is explained by each of these.

My guess is that it's a mix, and that the second one is real but maybe less important than people often assume. Part of why I say that is that as models get bigger and we do more clever things at inference time—chain of thought, retrieval, letting the model think for a while—a lot of the apparent gap in reasoning shrinks. The stuff that looked like a qualitatively different learning algorithm starts to look like something you can recover by running a big enough gradient-descent-trained model in the right way. That makes me suspect that the "humans are doing fundamentally different computation" story is weaker than it looks.

There's also a sense in which gradient descent is better than human learning that I think is worth saying. It's much more parallelizable, it can absorb a staggering amount of information, and it doesn't have the bottlenecks on memory and attention that humans have. So I don't think the right framing is really superiority in one direction. It's more that humans are extremely efficient on a small number of experiences and gradient descent is extremely scalable on a large number of them, and the interesting question is whether the scalable approach eventually gets the efficiency for free as you scale, or whether there's some trick evolution found that we still have to find ourselves. I lean toward thinking it mostly comes for free, but I'd hold that view with real uncertainty, and it matters a lot for timelines.

r001.rationale: The response says humans learn from far less data than modern language models and are more efficient per data point, but it does not state that humans become domain experts with less data than gradient descent would require under plausible trend extrapolations.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is that humans can use their understanding of what they’re doing to change how they learn. If I’m trying to get better at something, I can think, “What am I getting wrong? What would be a good exercise to practice? Is there someone who could explain this to me?” And that whole process is informed by everything else I know about the world.

Gradient descent is a much simpler procedure. It adjusts parameters in a direction that would have made the model do better on the examples it just saw. It doesn’t itself reason about why the model made a mistake or what it should study next.

But that’s not necessarily a limitation of systems trained with gradient descent. You could train a model that learns those same strategies—that can reflect on its mistakes, seek out useful information, and design exercises for itself. So I’d distinguish gradient descent as a learning algorithm from the learning that a system trained by gradient descent can do. The latter could, in principle, have all these advantages that human learning has.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human-directed learning strategies with gradient descent, but does not state that humans need much less data to become experts or mention plausible trend extrapolations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most striking thing is how much people can learn from a small amount of experience. If you explain a new game to me, I can use that explanation to make reasonable decisions before I’ve played very much. I don’t have to discover all the relevant concepts by repeatedly trying actions and getting a reward.

But it’s tricky to say how much of that is a better learning algorithm. A human has already spent years learning about the world, and evolution has done a lot of work to produce a brain that’s good at learning. So comparing a person learning a task to a neural network trained from scratch isn’t really fair.

The more interesting comparison is with a model that’s also had a huge amount of prior training. Then you can ask: how efficiently can it use an explanation, or a few examples, to do something new? Humans still seem better at some kinds of that, particularly when we need to figure out what matters and organize our own learning. But I don’t think that establishes some fundamental limitation of gradient descent.

r001.rationale: The response says humans can make reasonable decisions about a new game from little experience and may use explanations or examples efficiently. It does not claim humans need much less data to become domain experts than gradient descent would under plausible trend extrapolations.
